sources.title: Immigration's Effect on US Wages and Employment Redux
sources.table: Table 7 Panel A column 1, PDF page 41 (printed page 39)
sources.population: US national native/immigrant education-experience cells, 2000-2019; pooled genders, all workers, employment weighted; the 0.115 row concerns workers WITHOUT a high-school diploma.
sources.method: 2SLS relative weekly wages versus relative employment, education-specific coefficients, immigrant shift-share and native demographic instruments.
sources.transfer_limit: Transporting the no-diploma value to the broader hs_or_less cell is an assumption. The adjacent HS-diploma estimate is 0.017; the paper's own two-cell simulation uses inverse elasticity 0.045 for HS-or-less (PDF page 45), not 0.115. No parameter is estimated for Mexican-origin descendants or removal of a whole lineage.

sources.author: Suphanit Piyapromdee
sources.title: The Impact of Immigration on Wages, Internal Migration and Welfare
sources.table: Table 1 Panel I, PDF page 45 (printed page 45); sample definition PDF pages 6-7
sources.population: Low-skill means high-school graduates and dropouts, with separate gender/nativity nests. 114 US metropolitan areas plus an outside option; labor-demand estimation uses Census 1990/2000 and pooled ACS 2005-2007. Workers over 18, positive earnings, 1-40 years of potential experience, not in school; wage sample excludes self-employment and part-time/part-year workers.
sources.method: Instrumented spatial equilibrium labor-demand estimation; native/foreign-born substitution within low-skill and gender cells.
sources.transfer_limit: Transport to a national two-cell earnings-calibrated model pools gender and changes market, years, and population. The paper separately estimates high-skill nativity elasticity 6.925; this arm deliberately leaves above_hs infinite rather than transporting that estimate.

source_evidence.implementation_scope: Finite epsilon only in hs_or_less; above_hs infinite. High-skill wages may still move through cross-skill complementarity. Recompute descendant multipliers at each finite epsilon while holding the case's first-order descendant P/F increment fixed; that increment is an explicit allocation assumption, not a finite-epsilon descendant estimate.
